details:
**Jormungandr (the Midgard Serpent)**
The Norse "World Serpent," a child of Loki and the giantess Angrboda, which grew so large that it encircles the earth while biting its own tail. Thor once lifted it in disguise as a giant grey cat in Utgard-Loki's hall, and at Ragnarok Thor will kill it but walk only nine steps before dying from its venom.

**Thor's fishing trip with Hymir**
Thor went fishing with the giant Hymir, who refused to provide bait, so Thor tore the head off Hymir's largest ox and used it to hook Jormungandr. The frightened Hymir cut the line before Thor could kill the serpent; the scene is carved on stones such as the Hørdum Stone.

**Medusa's hair**
The Gorgon Medusa had living snakes in place of hair, and her gaze turned onlookers to stone. This is one of the most common giveaways for snakes in Greek myth.

**Nidhogg**
The Norse serpent or dragon that gnaws at the roots of the world tree Yggdrasil from the spring Hvergelmir in Niflheim. It is also said to chew on the corpses of the dead.

**Python at Delphi**
The serpent that guarded the site of Delphi, sent by Hera to hound the pregnant Leto so she could not give birth anywhere the sun shone. Leto's son Apollo later killed Python and took over Delphi as the site of his oracle.

**Tiresias and the mating snakes**
The Theban seer Tiresias came upon two mating snakes and struck one, which turned him into a woman for seven years. After striking a pair again he became a man, and he later angered Hera by telling her and Zeus that women enjoy sex more than men.

**The infant Heracles strangling snakes**
Hera sent two serpents into the cradle of the baby Heracles to kill him, but he strangled them with his bare hands. This was the first sign of his superhuman strength.

**Quetzalcoatl and Kukulkan (the feathered serpent)**
Quetzalcoatl is the feathered serpent god of the Aztecs, associated with wind and learning, whom Moctezuma II allegedly identified with Hernán Cortés; he departed on a raft of serpents. His Maya counterpart Kukulkan is honored at El Castillo in Chichen Itza, where shadows on the stairs form a serpent descending at the equinoxes.

**Laocoön and his sons**
The Trojan priest Laocoön warned the Trojans against accepting the Trojan Horse. Two sea serpents sent by a god (Poseidon or Athena in different versions) then came out of the sea and crushed him and his two sons.

**The ouroboros and the caduceus**
The ouroboros is the ancient symbol of a serpent eating its own tail, representing eternity and cyclic renewal. The caduceus is the herald's staff of Hermes, which has two snakes entwined around it.

**Nagas: Vasuki, Sesha, and Ananta**
Nagas are the divine serpent beings of Hindu mythology and the enemies of the eagle Garuda. The naga king Vasuki served as the churning rope wrapped around Mount Mandara during the churning of the Ocean of Milk, while the thousand-headed Sesha (also called Ananta) is the serpent on which Vishnu sleeps.

**Fafnir**
In Norse legend, Fafnir killed his father Hreidmar to take a cursed treasure including the ring Andvaranaut, then turned into a serpent or dragon to guard it. The hero Sigurd killed him at the instruction of Fafnir's brother Regin, and while roasting Fafnir's heart Sigurd tasted its blood and gained the ability to understand birds.

**Eurydice's death**
On her wedding day, Eurydice, the wife of Orpheus, was bitten by a snake while fleeing from Aristaeus and died. Orpheus then descended to the underworld to try to bring her back.

**Yamata no Orochi and Kusanagi**
In Japanese myth, the storm god Susanoo slew the eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent Yamata no Orochi after getting it drunk on sake, having turned the princess Kushinadahime into a comb to protect her. In one of its tails he found the sword Kusanagi ("Grass-Cutter"), which became one of Japan's imperial regalia.

**The Rainbow Serpent**
A creator figure in Australian Aboriginal mythology, associated with rain, water holes, fertility, and the cycle of life. It is said to have shaped the land and established laws during the Dreamtime.
